segments.text: We're used to software acting a certain way, but today's AI behaves entirely differently
from the apps and programs we've spent decades mastering.
If you expect an AI to act like traditional software, you are going to be confused.
That confusion usually comes down to two major differences.
First, AI learns patterns from examples, rather than just relying on explicit rules
written by a programmer.
Second, it can process messy, unstructured data, like everyday language or scribbled notes.
These two differences make AI far more capable than older systems in a lot of situations,
but they also make it much less predictable.
Let's say you're signing into Spotify, but you accidentally misspell your password.
Should the app let you in because you are close enough or had creative spelling?
Definitely not.
Traditional software doesn't do close enough.
It operates on strict, unbending instructions.
Just like a calculator running math or a spreadsheet executing a formula,
it follows a strict rule.
Let me in only if the password matches exactly.
This flowchart breaks down what rules look like.
A user enters a password.
If that password matches, the app opens.
Else, it throws an error.
Based on explicit instructions, it returns the exact same result every time it runs.
These rule-based systems are rigid and completely unforgiving,
but they offer perfect predictability.
That guarantee has been the foundation of computing for decades.
AI marks a shift in how software works.
Programmers still write the code that trains and runs the AI,
but they no longer write explicit instructions for every single answer it gives you.
This graphic offers an analogy.
On the left, rule-based software is a cooking robot following exact steps
to get the same result every time.
On the right, AI is a seasoned chef, recognizing patterns from thousands of dishes.
The chef doesn't need a recipe.
AI trades the robotic guarantee of identical repetition for a more human-like ability.
It adapts to entirely new, unscripted situations
using the patterns it learned during training.
Because traditional software relies on written rules,
it usually requires information to be fed to it in a specific organized format,
like rows and columns in a spreadsheet.
That's what we call structured data.
Look at the table on the left.
This structured data is a playlist, neatly organized into columns,
legible for traditional software.
On the right, the exact same playlist is unstructured data.
It's a messy, handwritten note with chaotic formatting,
instructional arrows, and crossed-out text.
A standard database would completely choke on this note.
AI makes sense of the mess by applying multiple layers of pattern recognition at once.
It decodes the handwriting, interprets the natural language,
and follows visual instructions, like arrows and crossed-out text.
That flexibility lets us communicate with computers the way we communicate with each other.
We can confidently feed an AI our raw, unformatted ideas,
and simply rely on it to make sense of the mess.
But that flexibility comes with a real cost.
Because AI makes decisions based on fluid, learned patterns rather than strict rules,
its thought process is inherently harder to predict and inspect than a simple password check.
Looking back at our messy, handwritten note,
an AI's pattern matching might just fail.
It might miss the visual cue and accidentally include
that crossed-out song in your final playlist anyway.
Its output can look incredibly polished, read with total confidence,
and still contain fundamental mistakes.
This message summarizes how we should navigate the new landscape.
Different jobs need different tools.
You have to choose the tool that fits the work.
AI isn't going to replace traditional software entirely,
and traditional software can't match AI's adaptability.
The key to modern productivity is simply knowing when your task demands
a rigid mathematical rule and when it needs a learned pattern.
